title: Ancient Egyptian Glass: From the Core-Formed Vessel to the Blowpipe
department: Department of Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations, Egyptology Program
description: An introduction to how the ancient Egyptians made faience and glass, for readers with no background in archaeology or chemistry. It is not a book about Egyptian glassblowing, because for most of Egyptian history nobody blew glass: Egyptians made glazed faience from Predynastic times and glass vessels from the New Kingdom (from the 15th century BC) by winding hot glass around a removable core or casting it in molds. Glassblowing was invented in the Syro-Palestinian region in the first century BC, spread under Rome, and only then made Roman Egypt, with Alexandria, a major glass center. The book follows that true story through real objects, excavated workshops, a Bronze Age shipwreck and the chemistry that tells where glass was made.
objectives: Explain what glass and Egyptian faience are made of and how they differ.
Describe step by step how core-formed and cast glass vessels were made in New Kingdom Egypt.
Use the excavated workshops at Amarna and Qantir-Piramesses to explain how Egyptians made and colored glass.
Explain how chemical analysis of the Uluburun glass ingots is used to trace Late Bronze Age glass trade, and why the results are debated.
State when and where glassblowing was invented and explain why it turned glass from a luxury into an everyday material.
Correct the claim that pharaonic Egyptians blew glass, citing dated evidence.

chapters.title: Faience: Egypt's First Shining Material
chapters.summary: What Egyptian faience is, how it was made from crushed quartz, and its long history from Predynastic times, long before true glass.
chapters.challenge: Find one faience object and one glass object in a museum's online collection and explain three ways to tell them apart.

sections.title: Glass and faience
sections.summary: Silica, flux and colorant, and why faience is a glazed body of crushed quartz rather than glass.

sections.title: Making faience
sections.summary: Shaping and molding, and the three ways a faience glaze could form: application, efflorescence and cementation.

sections.title: Faience through Egyptian history
sections.summary: From Predynastic beads to amulets, tiles, shabtis and the blue hippopotamus figures of the Middle Kingdom.

sections.title: How we know
sections.summary: Dating vitreous objects by context and inscriptions, and reading their making from their surfaces and chemistry, with the toolkit of ARC 101 Chapter 2.

chapters.title: The First Glass Vessels: Core-Forming and Casting
chapters.summary: How glass vessels appear in Egypt in the reign of Thutmose III in the 15th century BC, and how craftsmen built them around a core or cast them in molds.
chapters.challenge: Write illustrated, step-by-step instructions for making a core-formed vessel, then list the clues on a finished vessel that show it was not blown.

sections.title: Where glass vessels began
sections.summary: Core-formed vessels in Mesopotamia and Syria from about the middle of the 16th century BC, and how the craft reached Egypt.

sections.title: Glass under Thutmose III
sections.summary: The earliest Egyptian glass vessels, including a cup naming the king from the tomb of three of his foreign wives.

sections.title: Core-forming step by step
sections.summary: Building a core on a rod, trailing on hot glass, dragging the threads into zigzags, adding handles, and scraping out the core.

sections.title: Casting and cold-working
sections.summary: Glass pressed or cast in molds and finished by grinding and polishing, for inlays, amulets and small figures.

chapters.title: Workshops of the Pharaohs: Amarna and Qantir
chapters.summary: The excavated glassworks at Akhenaten's city of Amarna and at Qantir-Piramesses, Ramesses II's capital, and what they show about making and coloring glass.
chapters.challenge: Using the evidence from Amarna and Qantir, argue whether Egyptian workshops made glass from raw materials or only reworked imported glass.

sections.title: Brilliant things for Akhenaten
sections.summary: Paul Nicholson's excavation of site O45.1 at Amarna, where glass, faience, blue pigment and pottery were made side by side.

sections.title: Crucibles at Qantir
sections.summary: Hundreds of crucibles from about 1250 BC showing glass made from raw materials and colored, much of it red.

sections.title: Lapis lazuli from the kiln
sections.summary: How cobalt, copper and antimony compounds gave glass its blues, turquoise, reds, yellows and whites, imitating precious stones.

sections.title: Glass as a royal luxury
sections.summary: Who owned glass, how it was valued, and its place among the gifts exchanged between kings.

chapters.title: Glass on the Move: The Uluburun Ingots
chapters.summary: The glass ingots from the Uluburun shipwreck, the chemistry used to trace where they were made, and the decline of glassmaking at the end of the Bronze Age.
chapters.challenge: Given a table of trace-element results for four glass samples, group them by likely source and explain your reasoning.

sections.title: The Uluburun ship and its cargo
sections.summary: A Late Bronze Age wreck off the southern coast of Turkey carrying copper, tin and glass ingots in blue, turquoise and lavender.

sections.title: Fingerprinting glass
sections.summary: How trace elements in the sand and colorants can distinguish glass made in Egypt from glass made in Mesopotamia.

sections.title: An open question: whose glass?
sections.summary: A 2010 study of three ingots that pointed to Egypt, and a 2022 study of nearly the whole cargo that found most did not match Amarna.

sections.title: Decline at the end of the Bronze Age
sections.summary: Why glassmaking faded toward the end of the second millennium BC, and its later revival.

chapters.title: The Blowpipe Arrives: Glass in Roman Egypt
chapters.summary: How glassblowing was invented in the Syro-Palestinian region in the first century BC, spread under Rome, and helped make Roman Egypt and Alexandria great glass centers.
chapters.challenge: Write a 300-word museum label correcting the claim that pharaonic Egyptians blew glass, using at least three dated pieces of evidence from this book.

sections.title: Before the blowpipe
sections.summary: Cast and mosaic luxury glass of the Hellenistic world, often linked with Alexandria.

sections.title: The invention of glassblowing
sections.summary: The evidence that glass was first blown in the Syro-Palestinian region in the first century BC, and why blowing was so much faster.

sections.title: Glass for everyone
sections.summary: How free-blown and mold-blown glass, including vessels signed by Ennion, spread across the Roman world as everyday tableware and bottles.

sections.title: Roman Egypt as a glass center
sections.summary: Alexandria's glassworkers and Egypt's natron, the flux of Roman glass across the Mediterranean.

preface:
This book began with a question about Egyptian glassblowing, and the honest answer is the most interesting thing in it. For almost all of ancient Egyptian history, nobody anywhere blew glass. Egyptian craftsmen made shining blue faience for thousands of years, and from the reign of Thutmose III, in the 15th century BC, they made glass vessels by winding hot glass around a core or shaping it in molds. The blowpipe was invented much later, in the first century BC, on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean. Only after it reached Egypt under Roman rule did Alexandria become one of the great glass cities of the Roman world.

The five chapters follow that story in order: faience, the first glass vessels, the royal workshops at Amarna and Qantir, a Bronze Age shipwreck full of glass ingots, and finally the blowpipe. In each one you will look at real objects and real workshops, and learn how archaeologists date them and how chemistry can tell where a piece of glass was made. These are the same methods used in our books on ancient-astronaut claims (ARC 101) and on Sumer (ANE 101), so the three can be read together.

You do not need any chemistry, only curiosity and a museum website or two, because the challenges ask you to look closely at real objects. Please do not try to melt or work glass at home; it needs furnace heat and training. Looking closely is safe, and it will teach you more.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as an archaeological scientist would: from excavated workshops, dated objects in museum collections, chemical analyses and craft reconstruction, using the same dating and evidence methods as ARC 101 and ANE 101.
bible.promise: By the last page you will be able to look at a piece of ancient Egyptian faience or glass, say how and roughly when it was made, and explain why the blowpipe came so late in Egypt's story.
threads: Get the sequence right: faience, then core-formed and cast glass, then blowing, and what changed at each step.
Technique leaves traces: how an object was made can be read from its shape, surface and chemistry.

How we know: The archaeologist's toolkit, shared by ARC 101, EGY 101 and ANE 101: context (where a thing was found and with what), stratigraphy (lower layers are older), dating methods that check each other (radiocarbon, tree rings, inscriptions and king lists, styles of pottery and objects), materials analysis, written texts read in the original, and experimental archaeology.
Glass as artificial precious stone: color, value and display from faience to Roman tableware.

conventions: Use 'core-formed', 'cast', 'free-blown' and 'mold-blown' precisely; never call pre-Roman Egyptian glass 'blown'.
Dates as BC and AD with 'about' for approximate dates; give the evidence behind each key date (a royal name, a dated context, an analysis).
Kings by their usual Egyptological names (Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Ramesses II), with reign dates from the canon at first mention.
Metric units and degrees Celsius, each with a familiar comparison.
Cross-reference ARC 101 Chapter 2 and ANE 101 Chapter 1 for the shared dating and evidence methods.

bible.care: The reader asked about 'Ancient Egyptian glass blowing'. The book says plainly, in the description, the preface, Chapter 2 and Chapter 5, that glassblowing was not practiced in pharaonic Egypt: Egyptians made faience from Predynastic times and glass vessels by core-forming and casting from the New Kingdom, while the blowpipe was invented in the Syro-Palestinian region in the first century BC and reached Egypt under Roman rule. Treat this as correcting a very common assumption, not as the reader's mistake. Where specialists disagree (where glass was first made, how many stages glassmaking took at Amarna and Qantir, where the Uluburun ingots were made), present each view with its evidence. Safety: molten glass, furnaces and glass dust and shards are dangerous. Describe ancient methods, but never ask the reader to melt, blow or grind glass; challenges use drawings, museum collections and data.
